To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

primary progressive aphasia is a neurodegenerative disease, with a mean age at onset of 64 years, that is caused by a progressive degeneration of the left temporal lobe, with a mean survival after onset of 10 years.

primary progressive aphasia (PPA) is associated with a greater risk of transient global amnesia (TGA) compared with healthy control individuals and that the risk is not greater in PPA than in other neurodegenerative diseases.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of primary progressive aphasia and related neurodegenerative conditions, and their treatment and management.
the study of language disorders in the context of primary progressive aphasia (PPA), and the relationship between language and memory disorders in the context.
the development of a novel approach to the treatment of primary progressive aphasia and the treatment of transient global amnesia.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

transient global amnesia (TGA) is a syndrome of transient memory loss that occurs without any apparent cause, is not accompanied by other neurological deficits, and is associated with a benign clinical course and a good outcome.
there is no evidence to suggest that TGA is a risk factor for developing PPA.
there are no significant differences between the two disorders in terms of the clinical features, neuroimaging, and neurophysiological findings.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we found a high frequency of primary progressive aphasia in the patients with TGA.
we have identified the presence of an immune-mediated mechanism that can cause transient global amnesia (TGA) and that can be treated with immunosuppressant therapy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are two types of aphasia that have been associated with transient global amnesia, one that has a good outcome and one that has a poor outcome.
the clinical and neuroimaging features of TGA and PPA overlap, and that PPA may be misdiagnosed as TGA.
the clinical presentation of PPA and TGA can be similar.
